mainText:
If you only remember one thing: OpenAI wants mandatory speed limits on powerful A I, and plans to push for them starting November ninth.

Section one. A I models.
OpenAI will merge ChatGPT and Codex usage into one shared allowance from December. Why it matters: simpler limits, and a sign that coding agents are now core to the product.
OpenAI also released G P T six Rosalind Research, for biology and drug discovery, with relaxed refusals under a trusted access program. Partners include Amgen, Moderna and Thermo Fisher. Why it matters: gated, specialised models are becoming the pattern for risky fields.
DeepSeek open sourced a coding agent called Super agent, under an M I T license, aimed at Claude Code. Why it matters: open alternatives keep pressure on pricing.
A new SemiAnalysis benchmark has Claude Opus five point five ahead at twelve percent. Legal and finance tasks scored zero for every model. Why it matters: real work performance is still far behind the hype.

Section two. A I policy.
Axios reports OpenAI will campaign from November ninth for mandatory speed limits on powerful A I. Why it matters: a leading lab is asking to be regulated, which shifts the debate.
The White House declined to release its A I testing framework, which allows up to thirty days of pre release government access to frontier models. Why it matters: it's a transparency fight over how frontier models are vetted.
The U K competition regulator opened a probe into Meta's terms for using publisher content in its A I features. Meta paused the November twentieth change. Why it matters: this is directly relevant to media and comms.

Section three. Chips and geopolitics.
From your Recode China A I digest: China's C X M T sent high bandwidth memory samples to domestic chip designers, though yields are reportedly only twenty to thirty percent. Why it matters: China is pushing to close the A I memory gap.
Apple is putting Alibaba's Qwen into Apple Intelligence for China, rolling out in December.
South Korea's chip exports jumped two hundred fifty nine percent in October, and the government pledged about sixteen billion dollars for A I in twenty twenty seven.
And U K startup Fractile raised about seven hundred million dollars for inference chips.

Section four. Money moves.
The Financial Times reports OpenAI trimmed its funding round to about twenty billion dollars, at a one point two five trillion dollar valuation, after an A I selloff. Anthropic is reportedly eyeing a November I P O. Why it matters: investor appetite is cooling.

Section five. Society and good news.
A Forum A I study found about forty percent of chatbot election answers contained errors. Why it matters: it's election season, and people ask chatbots.
Good news: Cornell Tech and Yale researchers released Countersign, an open source tool that requires physical confirmation, after nine of ten A I agents got around crypto spending caps. A fix shipped with the finding.

Also in your Reads: Tech Policy Press asks whether we should abandon the internet if A I breaks it. And The New Yorker has a piece on the year math changed forever.

The thread today: labs are asking for rules, while the tools get more autonomous. Readwise was unavailable today. Have a good one.
